assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement of many neutral atoms and ultranarrow optical transitions. This gives fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, well beyond the microwave caesium standard, and enables tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. From a laser-spectroscopy and precision-measurement standpoint this is a clear, concrete instrument advance with obvious downstream science.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and carried out early realisations in strontium; Ye's group drove the record accuracy, stability and comparison work. Two laureates fits the supplied credit well. Related contributors such as ion-clock and comb developers have been recognised already (Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland 2012), so the credit here is cleanly bounded.
assessment.maturity: Strong and independent confirmation across many laboratories and species (Sr, Yb, Hg), with international clock comparisons and an ongoing roadmap toward a new SI second. Recognition is timely and the field is stable rather than speculative.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to pair the lattice clock with other clock technologies or wait for the formal redefinition of the second is uncertain.
I recall that other groups made important contributions to lattice-clock development, but the supplied credit lists only two names and I have not independently verified wider claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal of trapped-ion quantum gates and the broad programme of quantum information processing and simulation with controlled atoms and ions established a new experimental paradigm, from digital ion-trap computation to analogue and hybrid simulation. Originality of the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal is high and the experimental realisation is mature, though the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems (Haroche and Wineland) already covers part of the foundation.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the decisive theorists. Blatt is the leading experimental realiser of ion-trap quantum computing and simulation. Bloch is better matched to the neighbouring optical-lattice candidate, so leaving him off this entry avoids double use of credit under the three-person cap.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is extensive, with multi-qubit ion processors, error-correction demonstrations and commercial platforms. The theory-experiment pairing is mature and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the other atomic quantum-information candidates (B026, B037, B055) leaves the exact scope of a prize unresolved.
Whether Wineland-era ion-trap work is considered to already cover the experimental side is a judgement I cannot verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms and molecules turned the wave nature of atoms into a precision instrument, with applications in inertial sensing, gravimetry, measurement of the gravitational constant and fine-structure constant, and fundamental tests. It sits naturally next to laser cooling (1997) and BEC (2001) as an established atomic-physics instrument line.
assessment.attribution: Kasevich (with Chu) demonstrated light-pulse atom interferometers for inertial measurement; Pritchard developed atom interferometry with gratings and pioneered precision measurements. Mlynek shares early demonstration credit in 1991, so the three-person limit forces a difficult choice and credit is somewhat contested.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely reproduced, with growing deployment in gravity gradiometry and tests of the equivalence principle. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Allocation among Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich and Chu, who is not on the supplied list, is unresolved; the 1991 demonstrations were near-simultaneous.
Practical impact in field sensors is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution gave a physically secured communication protocol based on measurement disturbance and no-cloning, linking foundations to technology. The BB84 idea and later entanglement-based variants triggered an entire field of quantum cryptography and networks.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard is the decisive core contribution. Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is independently important and tempts a third name, but I would keep the pair for a tight, defensible attribution. Wiesner's early conjugate coding is not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Experimental QKD is widely demonstrated, including satellite links, and commercial systems exist. Security proofs and device-independence issues are still active, and practical impact is moderate. The 2022 prize already recognised entanglement and Bell tests, which partly overlaps.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize and with the foundational Bell-test credit.
Whether practical QKD deployment is judged sufficiently mature relative to the theory is uncertain.
Ekert credit versus Wiesner credit is an open attribution question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent light-matter interfaces, including cavity QED links, atomic-ensemble quantum memories and the quantum-repeater architecture, are the building blocks for quantum networks. This is close to my own work area of optical quantum memories, so I rate the physics highly but recognise I am close to the subject. The Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller and cavity-based network proposals created a clear, original blueprint.
assessment.attribution: Kimble led experimental realisation of quantum-network nodes, while Cirac and Zoller provided the theoretical architecture. Because Cirac and Zoller also appear in B010, only one such prize configuration is realistic. Memory experiments in crystals and ensembles involve many other groups not named here.
assessment.maturity: Elementary network links and memories have been demonstrated, but scalable repeaters and long-distance entanglement distribution are still under development. Recognition may be somewhat premature compared with the foundational theory.
uncertainties: Credit overlap with B010 and B004/B028 for Kimble and Cirac/Zoller.
Possible conflict of interest as my research includes quantum memories in rare-earth-doped crystals; I report this and weigh the candidate conservatively.
Maturity of the full quantum-network concept is incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables strong, controllable interactions between neutral atoms, supporting fast gates and programmable arrays of hundreds of atoms for quantum simulation and computing. The result is a rapidly growing platform with clear originality, linking atomic physics and many-body quantum science.
assessment.attribution: Lukin contributed the Rydberg-blockade proposal and large-array experiments; Browaeys and Saffman made key experimental demonstrations of blockade and gate operations. Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller and others proposed the original Rydberg gate concept and are not on this list, so the attribution is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Experimental progress is rapid and reproduced by several groups, but the field is still evolving and neutral-atom error correction is under development. Possibly premature relative to the oldest atomic-physics candidates.
uncertainties: Missing credit for the original Rydberg gate proposal (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller and colleagues) constrains a fair configuration.
Long-term impact for quantum computing is not yet settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light below the shot-noise limit in interferometers is a clear example of quantum-enhanced measurement. Caves proposed the idea in 1981 and its implementation in gravitational-wave detectors made a measurable difference. This resonates with the principle of improving what can be measured and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Caves is the theoretical originator of squeezing for interferometry. Schnabel led squeezing implementation work at GEO600 and beyond, and Mavalvala has major LIGO squeezing roles. Kimble's earlier squeezed-light experiments are important but compete with other candidates. The credit is difficult to bound at three.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so confirmation is strong. However, the 2017 prize for LIGO partly covers the sensor context, and recognition of an enabling technique may be considered secondary.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
Fair split among Caves, Kimble, Schnabel, Mavalvala and early experimentalists is difficult.
I did not verify specific squeezing-level figures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond opened solid-state quantum sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and strain at the nanoscale, including biological applications. This is a clear and original experimental advance with a growing practical footprint.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV optical detection and coherent control; Lukin contributed quantum-sensing and quantum-register concepts and experiments. Other groups, such as Awschalom and Hanson, also have strong claims and are not on the supplied list, so the attribution is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated across many groups and increasingly applied, but practical advantage over alternative sensors is still being established, and timing could be premature.
uncertainties: Missing contributors to NV physics make a three-person configuration contestable.
Lukin is also credited in B055, and committee practice may avoid repeated names.
Maturity of the sensing applications is mixed.
